subject: psych
title: Kitty Genovese and the bystander that wasn’t
dek: A 1964 murder in Kew Gardens, a Times story about 38 witnesses, a psychology of helping — and the later proof that the parable was not the night.

thumb.alt: Kew Gardens Long Island Rail Road platforms seen from a nearby bridge, 2020.

hero.alt: Train at the Kew Gardens LIRR platforms, photographed from the 82nd Avenue bridge in 2020.
hero.caption: Kew Gardens station, Queens, June 2020 — the railroad cut she parked beside in 1964. This is the place later. It is not a crime-scene photograph. The 1964 press pictures of the night are still under copyright; this capsule does not use them.

honesty: Catherine “Kitty” Genovese was murdered in Kew Gardens in the early hours of 13 March 1964. This capsule does not describe wounds or sexual violence. It does not use a police portrait of her or of the killer. The Times story of 27 March 1964 is treated as a primary source that later reporting — including the Times itself in 2016 — found flawed. The psychology that followed is real experimental work. The 38 silent witnesses are not.

timeline.label: Kew Gardens
timeline.detail: About 3:15 a.m.: Genovese is attacked near her apartment off Austin Street. She dies on the way to hospital.

timeline.label: A brief
timeline.detail: The Times runs a short item. The parable has not been written yet.

timeline.label: “37 Who Saw”
timeline.detail: Martin Gansberg’s front-page Times story. The headline says 37; the text says 38. None, it claims, called the police.

timeline.label: The lab
timeline.detail: Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: group size can inhibit helping. Diffusion of responsibility.

timeline.label: The parable
timeline.detail: Manning, Levine, and Collins in American Psychologist: no evidence for 38 witnesses, or that they watched, or that they all did nothing.

timeline.label: The paper of record
timeline.detail: The Times calls its 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” An editor’s note is later appended to the online 1964 story.

watch.title: Martin Gansberg — “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police” (The New York Times, 27 March 1964)
watch.note: The article that made the parable. Read it as a 1964 front page, then read the 2016 correction. The Times paywall may sit in front of the archive.

watch.title: Robert D. McFadden — Winston Moseley obituary (The New York Times, 4 April 2016)
watch.note: The Times’s own later account, including the judgment that the 1964 story “grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they had perceived.”

watch.title: Manning, Levine, and Collins — “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping” (American Psychologist, 2007)
watch.note: The paper that named the 38-witness story a parable. Abstract and DOI are public; the PDF may sit behind APA’s gate.

watch.title: Jim Rasenberger — “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (The New York Times, 8 February 2004)
watch.note: An early Times reconsideration, forty years on, before the 2007 journal article.

watch.title: NPR / All Things Considered — Kevin Cook, 3 March 2014
watch.note: Cook, author of a 2014 history of the case, on the police number and the interviews underneath it.

watch.title: WNYC — “An Iconic Murder Helped Create the 911 System” (2014)
watch.note: On the emergency-number afterlife. 911 was a national project; New York’s centralized number arrives later than the murder. The piece is a radio essay, not a statute.

glossary.explain: Born 7 July 1935 in Brooklyn; killed 13 March 1964 in Kew Gardens, Queens, at 28. She managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and lived on Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. The Times of 14 March 1964 is the first brief; the person is older than the parable.

A residential neighborhood in central Queens, around the Long Island Rail Road station and Austin Street. In 1964 it was also a short ride from the World’s Fair at Flushing Meadows. The murder is a Queens story that the Times turned into a story about the city.

The number the 27 March 1964 Times story made famous. The headline said 37; the body said 38. Manning, Levine, and Collins (2007) found no evidence that 38 people witnessed the murder. Kevin Cook later described a police compilation of interviews — some of them with more than one person in an apartment — that could be added up in more than one way.

The finding, from laboratory and field studies after 1964, that people are often less likely to help when others are present. Darley and Latané (1968) are the usual first citation. The effect does not require the Times’s 38 witnesses to be true. Textbooks that still open with those 38 as fact are telling the parable, not the experiment.

Darley and Latané’s term: in a group, each person feels less personally responsible for acting. The more people who could help, the easier it is to assume someone else will. It is a mechanism tested in labs. It is not a transcript of Austin Street.

Times metropolitan editor in 1964. He later wrote that Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy, over lunch, called the Queens killing “one for the books.” Rosenthal assigned the investigation that became Gansberg’s story and, the same year, published the short book Thirty-Eight Witnesses.

Times reporter whose 27 March 1964 piece carried the 37/38-witness claim and the neighbor’s line “I didn’t want to get involved.” Later journalists said other crime reporters already saw holes in the piece and did not take on Rosenthal.

Social psychologists. Their 1968 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology paper, “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility,” and the 1970 book The Unresponsive Bystander, built the experimental tradition that textbooks still teach. They started from the story the papers had already told.

A neighbor and friend who, after the second attack, went to Genovese, held her, and waited for the ambulance. The Times’s 2016 account names a woman who “cradled the dying victim.” Farrar’s Times obituary (2020) is the fuller named record. She is part of the night the parable left out.

Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins. American Psychologist, 2007: the 38-witness story is not supported by the archive. They separate that story from the bystander research tradition, which does not stand or fall with Gansberg’s count.

The U.S. centralized emergency number. In March 1964 New Yorkers reached the police by a precinct number or by dialing the operator. AT&T and the FCC announced a national 911 plan in 1968; New York City’s system came in after that. WNYC and PBS have told the Genovese story as one pressure among others for a single number. It was not a hotline created the week of the murder.

1960s press name for the idea that city life makes strangers indifferent. The Genovese story was fitted to it. Frances Cherry and others later argued that neighbors who heard a man and a woman at 3 a.m. often classified it as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the first parable did not pause for.

fun_fact.title: Thirty-seven, or thirty-eight
fun_fact.text: The Times headline of 27 March 1964 counted 37. The story under it counted 38. Reprints have used both. The slip is small and perfect: the number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed. What was stable was the moral — a city that would not pick up the phone.

sections.title: A quiet neighborhood, a loud city, no 911

blocks.text: Kew Gardens in 1964 was a Queens neighborhood of brick apartments, a Long Island Rail Road station, and Austin Street shops — statistically treated, then, as a safe borough compared with the Manhattan the magazines preferred to fear. Catherine Genovese, 28, managed a bar in Hollis and came home in the small hours. She shared an apartment at 82–70 Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. The city around them was in a year of other headlines: a World’s Fair opening in Flushing Meadows, a few stops away; a Civil Rights Act moving through Congress; a press already fond of the phrase “urban apathy.”

blocks.alt: Pedestrians, a City Omnibus bus, and stacked billboards on a Times Square sidewalk, about 1952.
blocks.caption: Times Square, May or June 1952 — Angelo Rizzuto, Library of Congress. A dozen years before the Kew Gardens story, this is the city’s publicity face: crowds, signs, the paper’s own neighborhood. The 1964 parable will treat the city as a crowd that will not move.
blocks.credit: Angelo Rizzuto / Library of Congress / no known restrictions

blocks.text: There was no 911. A neighbor who wanted the police dialed a precinct or the operator and hoped the line was free. That fact sits under every later sentence about people who “didn’t call.” Some people did try. The system they reached was not a single button.

sections.title: A night, then a front page, then a lab

blocks.text: In the early morning of 13 March 1964 Winston Moseley followed Genovese from the station parking lot and attacked her on the Austin Street side of the building. A neighbor, Robert Mozer, shouted; Moseley left and came back. The second attack was in a rear hallway, out of the street’s sight. Later reconstructions — Cook, the Times in 2016, the 2007 American Psychologist paper — agree on the shape: two attacks, not three; a layout that made a single continuous audience impossible; knife wounds that made a long, loud scream unlikely after the first blows. She was taken away by ambulance about 4:15 a.m. and died on the way to the hospital. Sophia Farrar, a neighbor, had gone to her and held her until help came.

blocks.alt: Kew Gardens LIRR station and the parking lot south of the tracks, seen from Lefferts Boulevard in 2019.
blocks.caption: The station and the south parking lot from Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019. Genovese parked in the railroad lot, about a hundred feet from the apartment door. The cars and the signage are of this century. The cut in the ground is the same fact.

blocks.text: The Times of 14 March ran a short notice. The story that lasted was assigned two weeks later, after Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy told metropolitan editor A. M. Rosenthal, over lunch, that the Queens case was “one for the books.” Martin Gansberg’s piece of 27 March 1964 went on page one: “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police.” The text said thirty-eight. It said they had watched. It said none had called. An unidentified neighbor supplied the line the decade needed: “I didn’t want to get involved.”

blocks.alt: A paved alley and stair from the Kew Gardens LIRR station toward Lefferts Boulevard, photographed in 2019, empty of people.
blocks.caption: The alley between the station and Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019 — the ground the case is attached to, in daylight, without a body. Wikipedia and the photographer’s caption treat this cut as the site. It is here as geography, not as evidence of what any window saw.

blocks.text: Social psychology moved faster than the corrections. John Darley and Bibb Latané designed emergencies in which a subject heard a seizure, or smoke, with or without other people present. In 1968 they reported, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, that groups inhibit intervention: diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance, the fear of doing the wrong thing in public. The 1970 book is called The Unresponsive Bystander. The Genovese name is in the preface of a field. The experiments do not need 38 silent windows. Many textbooks gave them those windows anyway.

Look outward from 1964, not only at one street. The World’s Fair opened in Queens that April. The Civil Rights Act passed in July. American newspapers were already running a story about cities as places where no one is anyone’s neighbor. Gansberg’s piece fitted a ready moral. That is one reason it was hard to unwrite.

sections.title: The woman, the editors, the experimenters, the neighbor

people.name: Catherine “Kitty” Genovese
people.text: A bartender and manager, a daughter of Brooklyn, a woman who lived with another woman on Austin Street. The photograph the papers circulated for years was a 1961 police picture from a bookmaking arrest. This capsule does not reprint it. She is not a mugshot and not a lesson in apathy. She is the person the story used.

people.name: A. M. Rosenthal and Martin Gansberg
people.text: Editor and reporter of the piece that turned a Queens homicide into a national character test. Rosenthal’s lunch with the commissioner is in his own later telling. Gansberg’s copy supplied the number and the quote. Other reporters, James Solomon’s later film The Witness records, already doubted the count and did not pick the fight.

people.name: John Darley and Bibb Latané
people.text: They built a research program out of a newspaper story. The program produced real, replicable effects about groups and helping. The debt to Gansberg is historical. It is not a reason to keep teaching his arithmetic as fact.

people.name: Sophia Farrar
people.text: The neighbor who went downstairs. The 2016 Times correction is careful and almost nameless (“a 70-year-old woman” — a number later writers have questioned). Farrar’s 2020 obituary is clearer: she held Genovese and said help was coming. The parable needed her not to exist.

sections.title: A discipline keeps a story, then some of it lets go

blocks.text: Moseley was convicted in June 1964 and died in prison in 2016. The story outlived him. Introductory textbooks in the United States and Britain used the 38 witnesses as a hook for decades. In 2007, in American Psychologist, Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins went back to the archive and wrote that there was “no evidence for the presence of 38 witnesses, or that witnesses observed the murder, or that witnesses remained inactive.” They asked the field to keep the experiments and retire the parable as history.

The Times, in 2016, called its second-day story flawed: the number was too high; no one saw the whole attack; many heard a quarrel and did not hear a murder; two people did call; someone went to the dying woman. In October 2016 an editor’s note was added to the online 1964 article. That is as close as a newspaper comes to walking back a founding myth of a social science.

What remains is not a shrug. Some neighbors did too little. Some classified a woman’s voice at 3 a.m. as private. The emergency number was a maze. The bystander literature is larger than one street and has been tested without Gansberg’s count. The teaching problem is the one this capsule is for: a discipline can be right about a mechanism and still be wrong about the story it uses to make students care.
If a field’s most famous example turns out to be a parable, what should it do with the example — drop it, label it, or keep using it because the experiment still works?
